reason: undici exists to control Node's global dispatcher so that fetch honours the proxy policy; in Go every outbound client is built by one factory on net/http with the policy applied per request, and bypass matching uses the x/net httpproxy package.

got is used only to make the OTLP telemetry request and its retry waits cancellable; a Go request takes a context that cancels all of that, and the client comes from the same factory so telemetry is proxied like everything else.

The multiplexed stream socket is dropped in favour of server-sent events; the one remaining WebSocket (the terminal) and any outbound WebSocket use github.com/coder/websocket behind a harness wrapper.
Opt-in gzip response compression is kept with the same exclusions and is provided by the gzhttp handler of klauspost/compress; the event stream is never compressed.
Its single use, choosing gzip or identity from Accept-Encoding, is done inside the chosen compression handler, so no separate negotiation library or parser is needed.
Serving a fixed directory of files to the owner is done by net/http file serving over an embedded io/fs file system, with a thin wrapper for method, header and directory rules.
Bind-address parsing and the wildcard and loopback checks move to net/netip, the same parser family the Go network stack binds with, which removes the upstream text-rewrite workaround.

Extension-to-type and type-to-extension lookups come from one media-type table compiled into the harness, because the standard mime lookup reads the Windows registry or system files and is not deterministic.
The Content-Type of a served workspace file comes from the same single media-type table as every other lookup, so the second upstream library has no counterpart.

Handing the entry URL to the default browser is done by starting the operating system's launcher directly with a scrubbed environment through os/exec, replacing the library and the extra Node process upstream wraps it in.
The test-only certificate fixture for the HTTPS listener is generated with crypto/x509 and crypto/ecdsa in a Go test helper; the product still never generates certificates.
It is a development command that previews upstream's separately built static client bundle; the Go UI is rendered by the host, so there is no standalone bundle to preview (upstream build process).
Listeners, route handlers, upgrades and header validation move to net/http with explicit time and size limits and owner-tracked connections, which Go does not provide by default.
The optional TLS listener uses crypto/tls with net/http; loading the certificate pair already fails on empty or mismatched files, so start-up fails closed without extra checks.
Unix sockets, half-close, IP-literal checks and inherited channels map to net, net/netip and os; Windows named pipes and Windows handle inheritance are stated gaps handed to the owning areas.
Its only product use is TLS with a pre-shared key for forwarded SSH streams; Go's crypto/tls has no pre-shared-key suites, so the same guarantee is given by TLS 1.3 with pinned one-time certificates.

The only imports are a failing stub of the Node module for the browser-worker preview and its test; no product code resolves names itself, and Go dials use the system resolver implicitly (Node built-in shim).
Nearly every use locates a JavaScript module by URL, which Go does not need; the few real conversions between paths and file URLs for a named target system become a small own helper beside net/url.

title: Outbound WebSocket clients bypass the proxy policy and no limitation records it
Proxying Node's built-in fetch depends on an undocumented global-dispatcher symbol shared with the npm copy of undici
An idle HTTP/2 session close surfaces as a process-fatal error, so callers disable HTTP/2 or install a socket guard
ipaddr.js and the socket layer read some IPv6 spellings differently, requiring a text rewrite and a hand-written wildcard test
selfsigned is held on 4.x because 5.x fails under pnpm with a duplicated ASN.1 package
User guide says web_fetch refuses literal private addresses while code and README say all addresses are reachable; stale connection-pinning comments remain
Browser hand-off runs the open library in a second Node process from a program string and works around its per-platform return timing
Two media-type libraries with separate tables (mime and mime-types) answer the same question in one product

reason: A WebSocket dial takes its http.Client from the one outbound client factory, so the proxy policy and certificate authorities apply to it as to every other request.
Go has no process-global dispatcher to patch; every client is constructed from the resolved policy, so no cross-version coupling exists.
The error is a property of undici combined with Node's uncaught-error handling; Go's HTTP/2 client closes idle connections without raising an error to the program (JavaScript runtime behaviour).
net/netip parses the dotted-tail spelling as the address the listener binds and reports only the all-zero address as unspecified, so one parser serves both classification and binding.
The pin exists because of how pnpm installs an npm dependency twice; Go's certificate generation is in the standard library and has no such dependency (npm packaging).
The client factory provides a connect-time destination guard and the security decision requires the fetch tool to use it, so the documented refusal of private addresses becomes real behaviour.
The host starts the operating system's launcher itself with a scrubbed environment and observes its exit code, so no second runtime or library-timing workaround is needed.
One media-type table in one Go package answers every lookup, and the UI is rendered by the host, so there is no second table in a client bundle.
